text: This lesson is one complete walk-through, combining an automation rule and a playbook on a single real scenario: a user-reported phishing email, moving from incident creation through notification without an analyst needing to start anything by hand.

A user forwards a suspicious email. A phishing-report analytics rule fires, and Sentinel creates an incident — Medium severity, the reporting user and the sender mapped as entities. Every automation rule watching for incident created now gets a chance to evaluate it. One rule, named Auto-notify SOC on phishing reports, checks whether this incident's analytics rule name matches the phishing detection. It does, so the rule's action fires: run the Notify-SOC-Teams playbook.

That condition is doing real work. If this had been a brute-force login alert instead, the condition would fail and nothing downstream would run — the rule only reaches this incident because its analytics rule name specifically matches a phishing report, exactly the scoping job a condition is supposed to do.

The playbook that runs is the Azure Logic App from two lessons ago. Its Microsoft Sentinel trigger receives the incident, then three actions run in order: get the incident's details — reporting user, sender, any extracted URLs; post a message into the SOC's Teams channel with the incident link and sender address; then add a tag back onto the incident so anyone opening it later can see this step already ran.

Notice what this playbook deliberately doesn't do. It doesn't auto-close the incident, and it doesn't take any action against the sender or the email itself. It only notifies and tags — it gets a human looking at the right incident faster, without ever deciding on its own that the email is malicious.

That restraint isn't an accident. Notify and tag versus take action on a judgment call is exactly the design question the next lesson covers: which actions are safe to fully automate, and which ones should always keep a human in the loop.
